questions.prompt: Which of these is a statistical question (one with varied answers)?
options: How many hours do students in my class sleep?
What colour is my school bag?
questions.explain: It expects different answers from different students.

questions.prompt: In the data 3, 5, 3, 2, 3, 5, 4, 3, what is the frequency of 3?
Data is grouped as 20–30, 30–40, 40–50. Where does 30 go?
questions.explain: Each class includes its lower limit but not its upper limit.

questions.prompt: A tally shows two groups of five and 3 single strokes. What is the frequency?
Why do the bars of a histogram touch, unlike a bar graph?
options: The class intervals are continuous, with no gaps between them
questions.explain: Heights run continuously from one class to the next.

questions.prompt: Heights: 140–145: 4 students, 145–150: 9, 150–155: 12, 155–160: 7. How many students are shorter than 150 cm?
Explain why the choice of class width matters when grouping data into a histogram.
questions.modelAnswer: If the classes are too narrow, there are many classes with only a few values in each, so the histogram looks bumpy and it's hard to see the overall pattern. If they are too wide, there are only one or two classes and the detail is lost. A sensible width (often giving about 5–10 classes) shows the shape of the data clearly.
rubric: Too narrow: bumpy, too many classes
A sensible choice shows the pattern

questions.prompt: Data you collect yourself (for example, by a survey) is called…
questions.explain: Secondary data comes from someone else's source.
